title: OCD 19 — Test
src: Clinical & radiographic findings of periodontal disease

mcqs.q: The primary etiologic factor for gingivitis is:
mcqs.explain: Plaque (biofilm) is the primary cause of gingivitis.

mcqs.q: Which finding is ABSENT in gingivitis but present in periodontitis?
mcqs.explain: Gingivitis shows no radiographic crestal bone loss; attachment/bone loss defines periodontitis.

mcqs.q: Gingivitis confined to the gingiva of a single tooth or group of teeth is termed:
mcqs.explain: Localized = one tooth/group; generalized = whole mouth; marginal/papillary/diffuse describe the part involved.

mcqs.q: The earliest signs of gingivitis most often appear in the:
mcqs.explain: Inflammation usually begins in the interdental papillae.

mcqs.q: Calculus is best defined as:
mcqs.explain: Calculus is mineralized plaque, usually covered by a layer of unmineralized plaque.

mcqs.q: The two earliest signs of gingival inflammation are increased crevicular fluid and:
mcqs.explain: Increased gingival crevicular fluid and bleeding on probing are the two earliest signs.

mcqs.q: Bleeding on probing is valuable because it:
opts: Appears earlier than colour change and is objective
Is the last sign to appear
mcqs.explain: BOP precedes visible colour change and is an objective sign useful for early diagnosis.

mcqs.q: Spontaneous gingival bleeding is most characteristic of:
mcqs.explain: Spontaneous bleeding suggests necrotizing gingivitis (and some systemic disorders).

mcqs.q: Which systemic factor can cause gingival bleeding?
mcqs.explain: Vitamin C/K deficiency, platelet disorders, leukaemia/haemophilia and anticoagulants cause bleeding.

mcqs.q: Gingiva appears RED when:
mcqs.explain: Increased vascularity or reduced keratinization makes gingiva red; reduced vascularity makes it pale.

mcqs.q: Loss of gingival stippling is:
mcqs.explain: Stippling indicates health; its loss is an early sign of inflammation (edema).

mcqs.q: Gingival recession is defined as:
opts: Exposure of the root by an apical shift of the gingiva
mcqs.explain: Recession = apical migration of the gingival margin exposing the root surface.

mcqs.q: A narrow, triangular gingival recession is called a:
mcqs.explain: A Stillman cleft is a narrow, triangular recession; a McCall festoon is a rolled, thickened band.

mcqs.q: A rolled, thickened band of gingiva (often near the cuspids) is a:
mcqs.explain: The McCall festoon is a rolled, thickened gingival band associated with inflammatory contour change.

mcqs.q: The feature that distinguishes periodontitis from gingivitis is:
mcqs.explain: Inflammatory clinical attachment loss (PDL + bone destruction) defines periodontitis.

mcqs.q: A periodontal pocket is a:
mcqs.explain: A pocket is a pathologically deepened sulcus from margin migration and/or attachment loss.

mcqs.q: A gingival (pseudo-)pocket is characterised by:
mcqs.explain: A gingival/pseudo-pocket deepens without destruction of the underlying periodontal tissues.

mcqs.q: A suprabony pocket has its base:
mcqs.explain: Suprabony = base coronal to bone; intrabony = base apical to bone.

mcqs.q: Spiral pockets are most commonly found in:
mcqs.explain: Spiral (complex) pockets twist around the tooth and are commonest in furcation areas.

mcqs.q: Periodontal pockets are usually:
mcqs.explain: Pockets are generally painless; signs include bluish-red margins, bleeding/suppuration and loose teeth.

mcqs.q: The only accurate method of detecting and measuring a periodontal pocket is:
opts: Careful probing with a periodontal probe
mcqs.explain: A periodontal probe is the only accurate way to detect and measure pocket depth.

mcqs.q: Clinical attachment loss is measured from the:
opts: CEJ to the base of the pocket
mcqs.explain: CAL uses the CEJ as the reference point, measured to the base of the pocket.

mcqs.q: When the gingival margin lies below (apical to) the CEJ, CAL equals:
mcqs.explain: With visible recession, CAL = probing depth + the gingival-margin-to-CEJ distance.

mcqs.q: Physiologic tooth mobility is approximately:
mcqs.explain: Physiologic mobility ≈ 0.2 mm horizontal and 0.02 mm axial; beyond this is pathologic.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the three main causes of tooth mobility?
mcqs.explain: The three causes are inflammation, attachment loss and occlusal trauma — not fluoride.

mcqs.q: Pathologic migration of teeth is an EARLY sign and is most frequent in the:
mcqs.explain: Pathologic migration is an early sign, most frequent in the anterior region.

mcqs.q: A full intraoral radiographic survey for periodontal diagnosis consists of:
mcqs.explain: A minimum of 14 periapical and 4 bitewing films is recommended; panoramic is only an overview.

mcqs.q: Regarding the earliest bone changes of periodontal disease, radiographs:
opts: Cannot capture them — they are detected clinically
mcqs.explain: Early demineralization is not visible radiographically; radiographs are an adjunct, not a substitute.

mcqs.q: Horizontal bone loss is characterised radiographically by a crest that is:
opts: Perpendicular to the long axis of adjacent teeth
mcqs.explain: Horizontal loss reduces interdental bone height with the crest perpendicular to the long axes; angular/vertical defects are arcuate.

mcqs.q: A widened periodontal ligament space on a radiograph suggests:
mcqs.explain: A widened PDL space is a classic radiographic sign of occlusal trauma.

mcqs.q: Identify the pattern of alveolar bone loss shown.
mcqs.explain: The radiographs show generalized horizontal and localized angular (vertical) alveolar bone loss.

mcqs.q: This diagram classifies pockets. The pocket whose base is apical to bone is:
mcqs.explain: The intrabony pocket has its base apical to the alveolar crest; suprabony is coronal to bone.

saqs.q: State the two earliest signs of gingival inflammation.
saqs.a: Increased gingival crevicular fluid and bleeding on gentle probing (BOP appears before colour change).

saqs.q: Define gingival recession and give two of its consequences.
saqs.a: Exposure of root by an apical shift of the gingiva. Consequences: root caries, sensitivity, pulpal hyperaemia, plaque retention, esthetics.
Suprabony — base coronal to the alveolar bone. Intrabony — base apical to the alveolar bone.

saqs.q: How is CAL calculated when the gingival margin is apical to the CEJ?
saqs.a: CAL = probing depth + recession (distance from CEJ to the gingival margin), i.e. X+Y.

saqs.q: Give the radiographic survey for periodontal diagnosis and one limitation of radiographs.
saqs.a: 14 intraoral + 4 bitewing films. Limitation: earliest bone changes are not visible radiographically (detect clinically).

saqs.q: Compare horizontal and angular (vertical) bone loss radiographically.
saqs.a: Horizontal: crest reduced but perpendicular to tooth long axes. Angular/vertical: arcuate (oblique) defect along the root.
